rows.finding: Direct deposits can be irrecoverable; `BulkSend` has no rescue surface
rows.plain_english: Anything sent directly to the contract, rather than through it, cannot be taken back out by anybody, including whoever wrote it.
rows.evidence: New `testDirectDepositsCanBeStuckDespiteNormalPathBeingNoncustodial`: direct ERC-20 transfer, unsafe ERC-721 deposit and forced ETH leave assets at BulkSend. `SelfRecipient` protects routed transfers only.
rows.minimal_fix: No contract change recommended. `SECURITY.md` already warns that deposits are lost. Adding rescue authority introduces a new trust policy; not a gas optimization.
rows.status: open limitation, no fix recommended by the report

rows.finding: `_mustBeNft`, `_mustNotBeNft`, `_answersOwnerOf` use uncapped staticcalls and dynamic returndata
rows.plain_english: A deliberately hostile token can burn the gas of the batch that names it while the contract is still working out what kind of token it is, which wastes that one sender's transaction and reaches nothing else.
rows.evidence: New `testLenientDoesNotBoundMaliciousClassificationCalls`: gas-burning fallback exhausts a bounded transaction before transfer iteration. A return bomb can similarly exhaust caller memory/gas. Requires selecting the hostile token; affects that caller's transaction, not other batches or approvals.
rows.minimal_fix: No blanket stipend cap recommended: it can reject expensive legitimate ownership probes. Treat the lenient guarantee as transfer-loop containment. A separately reviewed bounded classification policy is possible only if hostile-token support becomes a product requirement; normal-path savings unproven.
rows.status: open limitation, no fix recommended by the report

rows.finding: `_airdrop20` and NFT call-success counters do not prove economic delivery
rows.plain_english: A count of successful transfers is a count of calls that did not fail, and a token that accepts the call and moves nothing, or takes a cut, produces exactly the same count.
rows.evidence: Existing no-op, fee-on-transfer and impersonator fixtures show successful calls without exact requested receipts. A token can also lie in `balanceOf`, `ownerOf` or events. Classification is heuristic and can refuse hybrids/custom ERC-20 extensions.
rows.minimal_fix: Preserve post-transfer checks and held-row handling. No generic balance-check addition can authenticate an adversarial token. No production fix or gas saving claimed.
rows.status: open limitation, no fix recommended by the report

rows.finding: `_airdrop721(... safe=false ...)` can send NFTs to contracts unable to recover them
rows.plain_english: Turning off the safe-transfer box lets an NFT reach a contract that has no way to send it on again, which is why the box is on unless the sender turns it off.
rows.evidence: Existing deaf/wrong-magic/rejecting receiver tests distinguish unsafe transfers from safe callbacks.
rows.minimal_fix: Keep safe default and explicit user choice. Replacing safe transfers to save gas weakens recipient protection.
rows.status: open limitation, no fix recommended by the report

questions.answer: It sends an NFT or a token to hundreds of wallets in a few transactions instead of one at a time. When this started there was a bulk sender for ERC-20 on Robinhood Chain and nothing else, so anyone with an NFT collection or a set of ERC-1155 editions had no tool at all. It covers all three standards to the same standard, and it is free, open source and takes no fee. If your wallet can run several transfers as itself under EIP-5792, the page uses that route instead and BulkSend is never approved for anything.

They are adversarial review rounds, each by a fresh model given the code and no other context and asked to break it, published unedited including the unflattering parts. 22 rounds have run and 4 of them found no release blocker. The most recent demonstrated no critical, high or medium exploit and recorded four limitations instead, listed above with the report's own minimal fix beside each. These are not an audit in the sense a firm means it, and no human audit firm has reviewed this.

questions.q: How close is it to the gas floor?
questions.answer: The round-twenty-two benchmark built a minimal safe reference loop and measured real receipts against it on a local chain. At 300 recipients the current strict path costs between 0.12% and 0.72% more than that reference, depending on the token standard. The reference is not a mathematical lower bound; it is the cheapest loop that still keeps the safety properties this contract is for.

Because the measured savings are smaller than the risk of taking them. Three specialized prototypes were built and the best of them saved 0.73% at 100 recipients, while one was slower than the code it replaced. Each would need a new selector, a new deployment and its own differential fuzzing before it could ship. The one large saving, ascending NFT ordering, is already implemented in the page and needs no new bytecode.

questions.q: What is verified about the live deployment?
questions.answer: The runtime bytecode at 0x904412cfe982f33385f486aaff8c8a4a6f4b5fbf on Robinhood Chain mainnet was read back from the chain and is byte for byte what this repository builds, 9,752 bytes, and a second RPC endpoint was asked the same question at the same block and gave the same answer. The creation input matches the canonical initcode, there are no constructor arguments and no immutables, and the four constants and ten function selectors read from the live contract match the source. The page served at the live URL was compared with the file in this repository, and a scheduled workflow repeats that comparison four times a day from outside the thing being watched.

No. Every transfer is transferFrom with the original caller as the source, so the contract can only move what you approved, inside the transaction you signed, and nothing is ever held by it. There is no owner, no upgrade path, no fee and no pause. The one thing to know is the other side of that: there is no rescue function either, so anything sent directly to the contract rather than through it is lost, and for the two NFT standards the only approval either standard offers is setApprovalForAll, which is wider than the batch and lasts until you revoke it.

questions.q: What does strict versus lenient execution mean?
questions.answer: Strict is all or nothing: one recipient that cannot receive reverts the whole batch, nothing moves, and the token's own error is what you see. Lenient keeps going: a failing transfer is skipped and logged with its reason, the rest is delivered, and the call reports how many were sent and how many were skipped. Lenient also caps the gas each transfer may use, because without a cap one recipient whose hook burns everything starves the rest of the batch; the default is 400,000 gas and the WithGas entry points take a number between 100,000 and 5,000,000. Structural failures still revert the whole batch in both modes, including a zero amount, the contract itself as a recipient, and an ERC-20 answer that can be read as neither success nor failure.

questions.q: What are the current limitations and boundaries?
questions.answer: A delivery count means the token's transfer function was called and did not revert, which is not the same as somebody being paid: a contract that accepts the call and moves nothing looks identical from outside, and no on-chain check can tell the difference. The page asks the chain who holds what after every batch and reports a token that disagrees rather than counting it. Everything the pages show comes through one configured RPC endpoint, and a node can be stale or wrong while the block explorer is a separate reading to compare against, not proof. The duplicate ledger lives in one browser for one account, so another browser, another device or a cleared cache will not know about it, and the gas figures were measured for ordinary wallet recipients rather than for contracts with expensive receive hooks.
